title: reading notes: llm inference - zoe hart - kv cache & quant
content:
Quick notes from papers/blogs + ICLR 2025 talks (mostly scattershot). Intended as a scratchpad for experiments I want to run in the next sprint.

Top-level takeaways
- KV caching is the single biggest latency win for multi-turn chat if you can reuse cached past keys efficiently. Beware memory + eviction complexity for long-lived sessions.
- Quantization (GPTQ/LLM.int8/4-bit) gives big cost wins but changes distribution of logits; need targeted evals with representative prompts (not just perplexity).
- Continuous batching + prefix caching together can reduce p99 latency if routing + admission control are tuned.

Papers / talks I pulled notes from
- FlashAttention v2 (paper + talk): significant speedups on attention kernels; important when sequence lengths > 2k. Implementation detail: block-sizes and kernel fusion choices matter a lot on A100 vs H100.
- "KV Cache Sharding for Scalable Multi-Tenant Serving" (workshop talk): shard by session-id affinity, fallback to cold-shard for infrequent sessions. Eviction policy: LRU per-tenant + size-based trimming seems reasonable.
- "Practical 4-bit Quantization for LLMs" (arXiv): GPTQ variants keep most downstream quality but need calibration on a small eval set; some head/tail tokens more affected.

Concrete ideas to try on Redwood runtime (experiment list)
1) KV-cache memory profiling: instrument memory per-session with TTLs 5m/30m/24h and plot distribution. (linked JIRA: JIRA-RT-428)
2) Quantized candidate models: run 4-bit GPTQ build + run our reranking suite (search prompts, dialog prompts, code completion) to measure quality regressions. Use existing eval harness (github PR referenced above).
3) Prefix-caching + batching ablation: run A/B with and without prefix caching for median length 300 tokens; measure p50/p95/p99 and cost per 1M tokens.
4) Shard eviction sim: small sim to validate LRU per-tenant + size-trim heuristic (simulate 100k sessions, 5% heavy users).

Notes / questions (open)
- How do we handle cache invalidation when model rollouts change kv-format (e.g., different key shapes after a compilation change)? Should we version cache entries per-model-version and have transparent fallback to compute on miss?
- Prefix compression: are there cheap lossy compression schemes (quantize kv to 8-bit in cache) that reduce memory without hurting quality?
- Interaction with token-level tracing: need to ensure tracing doesn't blow up memory when we keep long-running sessions.

Quick heuristics from readings
- If >10% of requests are multi-turn with avg-turns > 4, prioritize KV cache: latency wins compound.
- For few-shot prompts with many context tokens, prefer FlashAttention optimizations over simple per-token quantization.
- Always run a small targeted eval set when trying a new quant config (50-200 prompts across tasks).

Links I want to follow up on
- Revisit FlashAttention implementation differences between XLA and CUDA kernels (notes in confluence link).
- Add quantized-model entries to model-catalog and tag them with quality metrics.
- Coordinate with runtime team (cc @Marco) on a small experiment to expose per-session mem metrics in the console.

TODOs

- [ ] Prototype per-session mem instrumentation (small PoC) -- assign: Marco -- due: 2025-04-18
- [ ] Create a short Confluence note summarizing eviction policy proposals -- assign: Aisha -- due: 2025-04-14

Notes-to-self style remarks
- Keep eval set diverse: not just code/completion, include customer-ish prompts (support, seo, summarization).
- Remember to measure prompt-engineering fallout: some prompts amplify quant errors.
- When running batch experiments, lock runtime config (batcher settings, kernel version) to ensure reproducible comparisons.

Random fragments I might expand later
- Small table: expected mem per 1k sessions vs TTL (5m/30m/24h) (can pull numbers from runtime PoC).
- Short blurb for eng-team: "Why KV cache matters for chat latency" (2-3 bullets + simple cost math).

End of scratchpad.
